name: Next-in-Line Effect
description: People often remember less of what happened immediately before their own turn to speak or perform. Anticipating one's upcoming turn can pull attention inward, so the just-preceding material never gets encoded well in the first place.
design_relevance_note: Most relevant to meetings, voice interfaces, collaborative tools, classroom/training software, and any turn-taking flow where users must prepare their own response while listening. Outside those contexts it is a narrow effect, not a general product-design law.
prevalence_note: A real textbook effect in social/cognitive psychology, but only rarely named explicitly in everyday product-design practice outside specialized turn-taking or training contexts.

findings.description: In turn-taking recall tasks, material presented immediately before a participant's own turn is remembered worse than other items, and the deficit behaves like an encoding failure rather than a retrieval failure because cues do not fix it while advance attention instructions can eliminate it.
findings.source_title: The next-in-line effect: Encoding or retrieval deficit?
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
